title: Kafka: a log, not a queue
dek: In 2011 three engineers at a large professional network described a messaging system that ignored most of what message queues did. No per-message acknowledgements and no deleting what was read: just an append-only log per partition, read by offset and kept for days. That one change made it fast enough for every click and log line, and it became the backbone of event-driven systems.

items: A topic is split into partitions, and each partition is an append-only log on disk. A message has no ID: it is known by its offset in the log.
Consumers pull from an offset they track themselves, and messages are kept for a set time (say 7 days) whether or not they were read. Anyone can read again from any point.
Because the broker only appends and hands out byte ranges, it is very fast: sequential disk writes, the operating system's page cache, and sending file data straight to the network.

body.x: The paper: "Kafka: a Distributed Messaging System for Log Processing" by Jay Kreps, Neha Narkhede and Jun Rao, NetDB 2011.

A large website produces a constant stream of events: page views, clicks, searches, and log lines from every server. The authors needed it in two places: in real-time systems such as feeds and abuse detection, and in batch jobs that load hours of data at a time. Traditional message queues tracked every message, acknowledged each one, and slowed down sharply when messages piled up unread. Log collectors handled volume but only in batches, hours later. Kafka set out to do both.

body.cap: The producer chooses the partition, often by hashing a key, so all of one restaurant's events stay in order in one partition. Consumers in a group divide the partitions between them; a separate group, such as analytics, reads the same data independently.

items: A partition is a set of segment files of about 1 GB. New messages are appended to the last one; nothing is ever changed in place.
A message is addressed by its offset, its position in the log. To consume, a client asks for 'messages from offset 9,120' and gets a batch back.
The broker keeps no record of who read what. Each consumer tracks its own offset; in 2011 the offsets lived in ZooKeeper.
Order is guaranteed only within a partition. A key that must stay ordered, such as one restaurant's orders, must always map to the same partition.
Delivery is at least once: after a crash a consumer resumes from its last saved offset and may see some messages twice, so processing should be safe to repeat.
Writes are sequential appends, the fastest thing a disk does, and both producers and consumers work in batches.
Kafka keeps no cache of its own and relies on the operating system's page cache, so recent messages are usually served from memory.
Sending a file to a socket uses the operating system's sendfile call, which skips copying the data through the application.
Because it doesn't track messages one by one, there is no per-message bookkeeping to slow it down as data piles up.

body.x: In the paper's tests a single producer sent 50,000 messages a second one at a time and 400,000 a second in batches of 50, several times the traditional queues it was compared with.

body.cap: Retention is by time, not by reading, so a consumer can be pointed back at an earlier offset. After fixing a bug, the search indexer re-reads yesterday's events and rebuilds its index; the order service doesn't have to send anything again.

body.x: This is the change that matters most. Because the log stays put, a new consumer can be added later and read from the start of retention, a batch job can load a whole day, and a buggy consumer can be fixed and replayed. A queue that deletes on read can't do any of that.

The 2011 version had no replication: if a broker's disk died, its partitions were lost. Replication arrived soon after, consumer offsets moved into Kafka itself, and later versions added transactions so a consumer could process and write results exactly once. Kafka became the usual backbone between services, and the idea of a durable, replayable log spread to many other systems.

items: Use a log when several independent services need the same events (notifications, search, analytics), when you may need to replay, or when volume is high. Use a simple queue when each job should be done once by one worker.
Choose the partition key for ordering: all events for one order or one restaurant go to the same partition.
The number of partitions caps parallelism: a group can't use more consumers than there are partitions.
Make consumers idempotent, because delivery is at least once.
Mention retention and replay as a recovery tool, as in the Notifications and Ad clicks problems.

body.label: Go deeper: why the broker doesn't track reads

body.x: Queues of the time recorded the state of every message (sent, delivered, acknowledged) so they could redeliver. That bookkeeping costs a write per message and grows with the backlog. Kafka moves the only state that matters, one offset per consumer per partition, to the consumer. The broker can then delete data by age alone, and a slow consumer costs the broker nothing but disk space.
